and yet no single interest of the people or any of the Legislature is more important than the preservation of this still noble and beneficent elf of Nature. The folly and rapacity of man have inflicted injuries which, if not absolutely irreparable, can be repaired only by the slow processes of time. And never before were the implements and agencies of destruction so numerous and so active as they now are. The latest appeal from this work of devastation is the intelligence of the people made by a number of eminent physicians, whose practice has impressed upon them the direct sanitary importance of the North Woods. Their indirect value to health and to commerce through their relations—the water-courses of the State—has been the subject of investigation and debate for years past. The point of view adopted by Dr. Loomis and his colleagues has not been urged so often. They deserve the thanks of the people, as does every one who makes an honest and intelligent plea in behalf of the Adirondacks. Their argument is that this region is a natural sanatorium—that it has no accessible counterparts; that one quarter of all the cases of incipient consumption subjected to its climatic influence may be, and under proper conditions are, in fact cured thereby; that the work of destruction is going on with constantly increasing force and effect, and that

The fact of the case is nowhere disputed so far as we know, except in the most strenuous manner by those who are immediately concerned in concealing them. The Forestry Commission reported the truth in May last a year ago, and recommended a simple and effective measure of preservation which was utterly ignored, during the year that has elapsed, additional injuries of immeasurable extent have been accomplished by lumber companies, and railroads, and more extended operations have been planned for the coming summer. The legislators have renewed their effort this session to procure the passage of a bill authorizing them to purchase such forest lands as they can buy for 90 cents an acre—a measure which unmistakably conceals no job and which is a practicable start in the right direction. This plan of salvation was defeated last year by the hostility of the representatives of the lumber counties, whose constituents are blinded by the present influx and circulation of capital to the inevitable consequence of reckless policy. This hostility would not have been effective, however, except for the stubborn indifference of legislators representing other parts of the State. These men have hitherto failed to see their duty and their immediate and pressing interest, but yet it is to them only that appeal can be made with any reasonable hope of success.

The principal agencies by which the perpetual use and enjoyment of the Adirondacks are being diverted from the whole people to the temporary advantage of individuals are, as we have said, the lumber industry and the railroads; and not only their interests, but their owners are largely identical in an enormously strong and an absolutely selfish combination. It carries with it everywhere a comprehensive system of devastation—by the axe, by fire, by the damming and diversion of water-courses, and by general transformation of conditions—that what was pure and lovely and healthful becomes foul and ugly and malarious, and every natural blessing is converted into a curse. It is nothing less than a dreadful calamity that Commonwealth possessing such a wonderful endowment and treasure should have permitted it to be squandered without pity or remorse and should still be blind to its own responsibility for such a miserable waste. The day will certainly come when this folly and sin will appear in its true light and proportions. There is great danger that it will come too late.

this year from New York next Thurs
day, June 10Th. On the afternoon of
that day the party will take the boat
for Albany and will arrive in that city
the next morning. They will remain
their until Monday and will then start
for Montreal by train. Arriving there
the same night the party will remain
until Saturday night, and on that even
ing they will take the night boat to
Quebec and arrive there on Sunday
morning. They will stay in Quebec
until Tuesday morning when they will
take the train to Fabian, White
Mountains, and will stay there until
Friday. This will give all who desire
an opportunity to take the trip up
Mount Washington, though this is
not included in the trip. On Friday
morning the editors will start for Bos-
ton and will have half day to look
about the "Hub," and they must hurry
to Fall River in time to take the
night boat to New York. They will
arrive in New York in time to get to
their homes before Sunday, The party
is to be limited to 200, and the tickets
cost $40. This is the most extensive
trip that the Association has taken in
years.

From Abilene: Reports of the actions of two clever swindlers come from the country districts. The men have been among the farmers, pretending to take orders for large alliance house in Kansas City, with prices marvelous in their cheapness. Samples were shown and were of the best quality. A cash payment of from $1 to $5 was exacted in advance, and, in most cases, paid. Needless to state there is no such house as represented and the goods never came. The rascals cleared several hundred dollars in this and neighboring counties.

Well, it is a curious story. On a farm adjoining the one on which I was born lived old Uncle Billy Christian, a good man and true as ever lived. Uncle Billy had a son who was a good deal older than myself. This young man was unfortunately afflicted with acute inflammatory rheumatism. New York, March 1, 1890.


Of course we will garnish our spring
head-gear with flowers. Of course we are!
But what flowers if we had only nature

would be confined to violets, lilies-of-the-

orchids, marigolds and few other
almost equally appropriate. Orchids, from
their comparative novelty, will undoubtedly
take. There is delightful unconvoc-

of any desired size, shape, color or
set of colors. It is so accommodating
which gives the artificial-manufacturer
neither trouble nor inquietude,

BLACK.


Among other things one observes about
spring millinery is that black will
certainly prevail. I do not mean to imply
that one is to assume mourning head-
gear, but black will figure largely in the com-
binations and will form the foundations of
most of the hats. With it will be combined
vivid cardinals and crimsons, and yellow
shades. These colors are much enhanced
by a black background, and black-and-red
or black-and-yellow combinations are de-
cidedly effective. Only, let our blonde
sisters beware.


YELLOW.


Yellow, in its faintest, palest tints will
be with us again and the designers are
showing much favor to biscuit, ecru, and
cream shades. Green in many gradations
is also in the gamut of vernal millinery
colorings. Teal, too, heliotrope is fash-
ionable once more, and the two match
effectively.

large for exhaustive discussion in the space
allotted to me. Suffice it to say, nothing

fashionable, except it be a Spanish man-
illa. In hats large, eccentric, daringly,
picturesque forms are prescribed. Cam-
bridges, Bolero, and Torador modes,

and they are of the closest, smallest va-
riety of course they are denominated
English touques. The bonnet proper has
not a fair field. Even the capote, which
rarely beholds the frowning side of Dame
Fashion's countenance, does not seem so
popular as usual. For evening wear it will
of course be employed, but even here it has
to compete with the toque.


DRESSES.


The dinner-gown, par excellence, is a
princess model in draped gauze. It has a
bewitching sash girdle of embroidered ope-
ra china, loosely finished with deep
falls of lace and a petticoat of silk velvet.
Plaids will accompany us into the next
season, but their designs will be less pro-
tracted; many will be two-tone figures.

wears, which are to have few days airing
before coming back to their native camphor.

will have the cutaway effect in front, with
long tail behind, which is relic of the
directoire vogue. These coats are cut-away

coats beneath. As the season advances
this waistcoat will be of percale and dis-

will not appear in it, nor will Juan in the epi-
max disappear through trap in the glare of
sulphurous flames.


The only New York novelty in the theatrical
line last week was Fanny Davenport's produc-
tion of Cleopatra — in which Sarah Bernhardt
is said to have been a failure.
If the consensus of metropolitan
criticism is to be trusted, there is not much in
the play or in Miss Davenport's embodiment of
the Egyptian heroine to please American audi-
ences. The dresses and the undressing of
Cleopatra are much talked of, but these feat-
ures and Miss Davenport's knowledge of her
art alone seem to have saved the play from
failure. Sardou's work in Cleopatra is not
at all commended, and William Winter sums
up the case in the New York Tribune as fol-
lows: Miss Davenport makes a good whole-
some, domestic Bostonian or Philadelphia
Cleopatra, who would really do not one of the
naughty deeds of the enchanting Egyptian but
rather would have married Antony and settled
him as Chief Justice of Alexandria. Mr. Mel-
bourne McDowell, heavy man, with vast laws
and ill-looking countenance, presented Antony
and created frequent disturbances.


Stuart Robson says that comedy is the most
serious business in the world. If he is think-
ing of that deplorable question as Marriage a
Failure, Mr. Robson states the truth mildly.
The dialect comedy craze is spreading just as
the dialect poetry overwhelmed us for time
after James Whitcomb Riley made it a thing
of beauty and joy so long as he held the pen.
Manager Jacob List gave for the first time at
Troy, N.Y., on Christmas Day, "Lyon Yonson,"
a drama full of Swedish-American dialect and
dealing with life in the lumbering district in
the Northwest. A realistic representation of a
log jam is said to have had more to do with
it than the Swedish.
The lovely Lillian Russell is embarrassed
with good fortune. According to stories cur-
rent in theatrical circles this week the comic
opera prima donna is in doubt whether to re-
main with Mr. Aronson at the New York Ca-
sinO at salary said to be $500 a week, to accep-
Manager French's offer of $500 a week to play
at the Garden Theater, or to star by herself in
company that an amiable gentleman whose
name is not mentioned, but who is possessed of
wealth untold, has offered to organize for her.
She refuses to say which path she intends to
take, but as all lead to fortune for her at all
events she can afford to let the managers and
the hackers in prospective do the worrying.


Another rumor about the fairy Lillian is that
she is once more contemplating a matrimonial
alliance. The happy man who is said to be the
object of her choice is the same heroic person
who has offered to raise a great comic opera
company for her. As is usual in such cases
he is described as a wealthy bachelor engaged
in fighting in Wall street. If he ever resolves
into substantial reality at the altar he will be
Miss Russell's husband. Her friends do
not believe in the matrimonial story but it has
been her way to do the unexpected thing at all
times, and there is no reason why a man who
is willing to try to manage her should not be
daring enough to marry her.


In spite of the unfavorable criticisms, Mar-
garet Mather's "Joan of Arc" is said to have at-
tracted large audiences in New York. Mana-
ger Gulick, of the Bijou Theater saw the piece
when he was in New York last week, and tells
me that its spectacular power at all events is
very great. The house was crowded the night
he was there, and Margaret Mather was re-
called at the end of every act. New York judg-
ment is not infallible, and maybe Pittsburg,
which has always been very partial to Miss
Mather, will take more kindly to Joan of Arc.
It will be seen here shortly.


Comic opera, light comedy and melodrama
are the staple attractions at the theaters this
week. "Poor Jonathan" has the reputation of
being a good deal of a novelty in the way of
plot, costuming and action. It is modern
in every way. "All the Comforts of Home" is
a farce comedy in the real meaning of the word,
half way between comedy and farce. After
Dark is a melodrama too well known to need
description, and the other theaters have
familiar attractions also.

Kansas City, July 8.—Frank Terry, W. I., F. I. Co. express messenger, his helper and a baggage man had a thrilling experience on a Santa Fe train near Argentine yesterday with a mammoth seal, which, with three others, had been shipped from San Francisco to New York.

There were two pairs of the seal and they had been brought down from the seal islands in the Pacific for the owner of a geological garden in New York. The animals were taken from the ship where they had been in water and shipped in three large wooden cages, well constructed and strongly bound by hemp ropes to doubly insure against the possibility of their breaking out.

He jumped on a large pile of express matter but was quickly driven from that position. The men at last made their escape through the side door of the car and closed it behind them. The seal raged for about five minutes and then dropped down dead. The carcass, weighing 518 pounds, was taken to Armour's packing house and skinned.

The remaining seal was carefully watered here this morning and shipped on to New York.

Washington, Aug. 6.—Before the reading of the bill in the House today, Mr. Holman of Indiana raised the point of no quorum on motion. A call of the House was ordered, which disclosed the presence of only 15. The sergeant at Arms was directed to hunt up an absentee, and the House relapsed into state of recess, while struggles came in the presence of the clerk.

At 2 o'clock in the afternoon when a quorum appeared and, further proceedings having been dispensed with, the Journal was read.

The House then resumed in the morning hour, the consideration of the bill exempting mining from the provisions of the Allen Land law.

Mr. Holman of Indiana, opposed the measure, expressing the wish that all agricultural lands and mineral lands, all the solid wealth of our country, should be held by American citizens.

Mr. Payson of Illinois, characterized as gratuitous the statement made yesterday by Mr. Carter of Missouri that pending the discussion of the Allen Land law the question of the ownership of mining property had not been considered. He had been earnestly considered he was opposed to the pending measure, implying his opposition upon the broad principle that American lands should be kept for Americans only.

Mr. Smith of Arizona, said that the people of Arizona were fully as American and patriotic as were the people represented by the gentlemen from Illinois and Indiana (Mr. Payson and Mr. Holman). It was simple justice. To make a law equal was American policy.

Mr. Holman moved to lay the bill on the table. Agreed—20 yeas, 10 nays.

The House then proceeded, under the special order, to the consideration of the Senate bill providing for the inspection of meats for export.

Mr. Funston of Kansas, chairman of the committee on Agriculture, expressed his pleasure in being able to advocate the measure, upon the dependence on removal of the restrictions of foreign governments which to a great degree had embarrassed the large agricultural interests of this country.

Mr. Morgan of Mississippi, diverged from the subject in hand to denounce the action of the Agricultural Committee in reporting the Compound Lard bill, which singled out for attack one article of commerce; as for the pending bill he objected that it did not include lard among the products which were to receive a certificate of character.

The plea is often made by business men
that it will NOT do for them to express
any political preference because it will
injure their business. This is urged fire.
quently as an excuse for neglect of the
plain duty of every American citizen-to
participate more or less actively in polit-
ical campaigns, at least to the extent of
expressing their principles at the polls.
This is not only fallocious but democrat
izing. No one thinks less of man for
entertaining honest convictions, and Civ
ing reasonable expression to them, no
matter how widely he may differ in opin-
ion. Trade is not governed by political
preference. Ono is not influenced in the
purchase of a pound of tea or a suit of
clothes by the political opinion of the
merchant who sells them. On the con-
trary everybody admires the man who
has pronounced principles and is not
afraid or ashamed to give them moderate
and courteous expression. Social and
business relations are not determined up
on any such basis. All of us have the
warmest of friends who do not agree
with us politically. and we think none of
the less of them on that account, and yet
there are good business men of both po-
litical parties in this city who are driven
from active participation in politics for
fear they will loose custom.

April 25.—Congressman Brinkindgs stated yesterday that in his opinion he line had arrived when the Governor of Arkansas should remove the veil of secrecy he has guarded his operations in the matter of John N. special Court of Claims invested with jurisdiction to try these cases, and then the matter would rest until the succeeding session—claimants waiting and suffering. The present movement is only a renewal of the agitation con-

cerning the oft proposed court and will be readily disposed of in the same manner. If this is the best that can be done, adopt it at once and end the long anxiety of the claimants. But inasmuch as the testimony in support of these claims was taken years ago, to be used before the department authorized to decide as to its sufficien-

cy, and as many of the witnesses and some of the claimants are dead, or beyond the seas with small prospects of supplying their evidence, to meet the ends of justice, it would seem preferable that the department should still be the tribunal to examine the testimony submitted and deter-

mine the amounts, to be followed by necessary appropriations.

If this is not practicable, instead of creating a new court, confer jurisdic-

tion on the Federal District Courts held within the Territory, to hear such

cases in each county, or at least within the district, and at such hearing,

accept the testimony already taken with such additional proof as might be required. Impartial justice could thus be obtained. Heard in the vicin-

ity of where the depreciation was com-

mitted, both the government and the claimant would have better opportu-

nities to ascertain the fraud or merit of the claim. If, however, the national capitol longeth to become the abid-

ing place of some seedy aspirant, for whom no other vacancy can be found, let the new court be created, provided always, that the testimony now on file shall be accepted as proof subject only to rebuttal. Without such a pro-

vision, with witnesses scattered, some claimants dead, proof lost, evidence forgotten, papers pigeon-

holed, the court far distant, and attorneys not familiar with the facts, it would be extreme folly for the old and impov-

erished claimant to expect anything.

It would be preferable and more honorable for the government to plead the statute of limitation and at once make final disposition of the cases. In addition to the loss of life, abandonment of homes, etc., the ac-

tual loss within the Territory has been serious, especially so in the counties adjacent to the reservations and those

traversed by the bloody trails of the hostiles. The aggregate of claims of residents of Gila county approximate $40,000—small compensation to suffer-

ers who have presented demands, and

falls far short of the actual loss, if any estimate is to be made for those who declined to make any demand on ac-

count of the slow process, and improb-

ability of collection. This matter de-

serves serious consideration and speedy

action.

Taken all in all the War of the Rebellion was the greatest war in history. There have been long wars, there have been wars which were from first to last more destructive of human life. But there have been no wars in which the combatants were more evenly matched. There have been none of 80 desperate fighting and of 80 sanguinary results for the multitude.

Those who fought on either side belonged to the same great race. No braver and more enduring men ever met in shock of battle than those who faced each other on a hundred fields. The losses on either side in many of those conflicts bear fearful witness to the staying qualities of the men engaged, and the destructive characters of the war.

Waterloo is called one of the world's great conflicts. Without doubt it was. But there are a dozen battles of the Rebellion which show much larger percentage of killed or wounded.

There were companies of men on both sides which lost in single battle more than 80 per cent of the men engaged. There was a company which took part in Pickett's grand and desperate charge at Gettysburg in which every man was either killed or wounded. What an awful and thrilling story do such facts tell of the deadly character of the struggle.

The approach of the Nation's Memorial Day especially calls to mind the patriotic self-sacrifice which was a preeminent character of the war. By what power have the ideas of modern civilization been propagated? By the principle which was illustrated in its widest application by the death of Christ upon the cross, a sublime principle of self-sacrifice. Upon the cross of Calvary the climactic Man of all the glories who was also the Son of God, gave his life for the salvation and moral uplifting of the race.

Through the power of that transcendent example has man been moving upwards. Man has labored and toiled and sacrificed and we have entered into their labors.

How much we owe to this great principle of self-sacrifice. Even the right to gather here this morning in quietness and peace for Christian worship has not yet been bought without the price of sacrifice. Men have been persecuted and have shed their blood.

To secure liberty of conscience, and freedom to worship God, our American Republic, this greatest experiment of self-government, was born of the power of this principle. Upon the fields of Lexington and Bunker Hill, Bennington and Monmouth, Princeton and Germantown, Saratoga and Yorktown were fought the battles of a higher and altar freedom. The blood of the best and bravest of the sons of the revolution moistened the soil which henceforth became hallowed ground. By untold self-sacrifice have the liberties there won been preserved and transmitted unto us.

There came a time when the life of the Nation was at stake. Many of us recall the appeal of patriotic indignation that swept like wild fire through the land when our Nation's flag was defiled. Then was witnessed a proud uprising in behalf of the stars and stripes. The best and most dignified went forth to fight the war.

man, in an interview here, said that the

victory of the Democracy was an ex-

radical."

they are cautious and conservative, they

The idea of unlimited acres, and
farm operations on a large scale, is
very attractive to some tillers of the
soil, particularly those who are
young. There are two sides to this
question, however, as to most others.
If one has large capital, he can, of
course, extend his business to any
limit that seems profitable, but for
the farmer whose only capital is the
small farm he owns,the wisest course
is to crowd that little farm to its ut
most limit of productiveness, before
he seeks to acquire more land, unless
it be an exceptional case where large
returns are certain.


Note some of the points of advan-
tage in working a small but rich
farm. The taxes are less than on
larger farm that is no more produc-
tive in total results. The expense of
working the smaller place will be
much less. The actual labor requir-
ed on the part of the farmer himself
will be less. He will be freed from
the constant worry and care that
accompany the cultivation of large
areas. Less hired help will be need
ed. There will be fewer fences to
keep in repair and less expense for
fertilizers when there is concentra-
ton Of these.


Now given the small place in a fair
state of productiveness, let US see if
better farming on the present area
cannot be made profitable. When
the soil has been properly prepared
for the crop, and the usual amount of
dressing applied, the farmer is at q
point when he can say, "Shall 1 put
in this crop and get the usual aver
age results, or shall l double the
yield by increased cultivation and
increased fertilization?"


Barring accidents that are outside
of mans control, the ordinary yield
can be doubled without doubling the
labor or the amount of dressing. A
certain amount of plant food is neces-
sary to start the crop and produce the
stalk. If the supply gives out at this
point, there will be small returns at
harvest time. 1t is just here that so
much failure occurs in farming. The
expense of preparing the soil and fur
nishing certain amount of dressing
is incurred and here the planter
stops, as also does his crop. 1t is the
extra feed beyond that which is re-
quired to produce the plant itself
that pays. Better put all the fertil-
izer and all the cultivation on a small

This little paper is never heard of on this side of the water except when it is approvingly quoted by our protectionist organ, the "American Economist," to show, forsooth, that England is going to adopt the great protectionist system. It may be said in passing that it is a most singular thing to see the Economist expressing pleasure over what it fancies to be the growth of protection in England. The Economist ought to know that more than half of our exports go to England, and that the adoption of protection there would be very harmful to us—especially to our farmers who produce about three-fourths of our exports.

The "Fair Traders" consider the present policy of England in trading with other nations without any custom-house restrictions to be unjust and unfair. The goods of all countries are admitted free into England, except a few revenue articles; but nearly everything manufactured and exported by England has to meet heavy duties upon passing into other nations. This the "Fair Traders" say is unfair, and they propose to make it fair, and hence their name.

But how DO they propose to make it fair? Let us take an illustration from our treasury reports for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1889. upper gateway of the great canyon


as if by its very frown to keep back


the intruder and guard from vulgar


eyes and sordid greed the grandeur,


the beauty and hidden treasure OF


the lower canyon. At the Bright


Angel Creek everything changes
the granite slopes are f1atter, they


are of softer black granite, cut into
sharp pinnacles and crags, and seem


more as if formed of very coarsely


stratified slate.


The canyon grows more and more
picturesque and beautiful the farther
we proceed. The granite has lost its
awful and threatening look and slopes


back in beautiful hillsides of variega-
ted black, gray and green.

bends of the river, the upper portions

view, showing the great marble and
sandstone cliffs, benched back far

ther, and higher and higher, and in
immensely OF height and proportion

heads. First above the dark sand

black, and the little benches between

whole crowned with perhaps couple
of thousand feet of the lighter gray,
yellow and white sandstone lodges,
capped by pinnacles and spires, tur-
rents and domes, in every imaginable
shade, size aud proportion.

She was also very averse to society, for the runaway marriage made her delicately sensitive about society in the beginning, and at last it became distasteful to her. Curiously enough their eldest daughter married without the consent of her parents.

The story of Southey's love and marriage can never be absent from such a compilation of this sort. No man ever had less right to get married than Southey. He had no money, no profession, no place in the world, and, more than this, he was dependent on his friend Cottle, who had been supplying him with money. Cottle had to supply him even with the ring and the money for the wedding. After that beginning he lived a long life of anxious earnest literary labor, earning not much, winning no great fame, but leaving behind him a memory rich in every sort of private virtue and worth. No doubt his wife, both as bride and during all her life, had much the heaviest part of the daily burden to bear. She bore it nobly, and died, indeed, a martyr to duty toward her husband and children, her last days being clouded by mental troubles which caused her to be secluded. Forty years had they been married when Edith died. Southey's own life was not to be long, and his last days were also passed in gentle mental alienation which continued till he died.

He was absolutely without morality, and almost without decency, for he dragged to his wife of his early amours and successes till she was forced, in self-defence, to close his mouth with an effective sarcasm.

Among the disappointed men of genius may be mentioned Buckle, the historian of civilizations; Henry Fielding, the novelist; Edward Gibbon, the historian; Lord Mansfield, and, in early life, John Wesley. Thursday night, the 31st, while the S. S. Crockett, Captain Thorndyke, was lying on the north side of the dock, some one entered the cabin and held and depleted the wardrobes of the jolly tars. Trousers, suspenders, shoes, and shirts shared the same fate, and downtown clothing merchants the next day were happy. Last Thursday night another visitation was made. Captain Thorndyke had sought to the seclusion which the cabin grants and was wooing Norpheles when a match was struck.

The lighted stick was immediately held over his face, and he saw the unwei visage of darkey. The Captain immediately jumped on his intruder, and a scuffle ensued. No code of rules were observed, and the fight was a determined one from start to finish. The darkey, however, succeeded in getting away, and carried a suit of the captain's best Sunday clothes with him.

On the previous occasion the darkey stole a double-faced gold watch. This he sent to Stern's pawnbroker shop Saturday night by a white boy to have it pawned. Mr. Stern told the boy that he had received notice that the watch had been stolen, and could not pawn it. Hawkins standing outside left the building and was pursued by an officer. The crowd about the place, however, impeded locomotion, and Hawkins escaped. Captain Foster of the Annie Allen has also suffered by the depredations of the same. Clothing has been the chief thing, but enough to stock a second-class store has been taken from the Allen. It seems that Hawkins lived at 81 Byrd street during the day, spent the early part of the night tricking and stealing the sailors' clothes when they were wrapped in slumber. During the day Hawkins was something of a dude. He never passed a day that he did not don three suits of clothes, and several days this week four suits have been his ratio. At his house a great deal of the stolen property was recovered last night by Officer Hall—four or five suits of clothes, two pair of shoes, towels, valise and other appurtenances were found, and the watch of Captain Thorndyke was also taken from him.

Both the latter and Captain Foster identified some of the clothing as belonging to their ships, and Captain Thorndyke, at the first station last night, identified Hawkins as the man with whom he had the tussle Thursday night.

A portion of the stolen goods yet remains unidentified, but will evidently be at the Police Court today. All the sailors and shippers will be on hand, and a preliminary examination at court will be gone into.

It is not easy to say where tipping ends and downright bribery begins, any more than it is easy to decide at what point on the social scale one may cease to tip. Each of these points is illustrated by true stories of English life. An American travelling in Great Britain fell into conversation with an Englishman, and presently, of course, was listening to him rail against corruption in American politics. The American bore it all patiently and acknowledged the truth of many charges brought by his companion, but finally asked whether there was no corruption in English politics. "Some; but not so much as in yours" was the answer. "Any bribery?" pursued the American. The Englishman's face changed, and then, with a smile, he admitted that there was. In fact, he had met with it in his own experience. Supplies furnished by him to the Government had been rejected on the ground that they were not of the specified quality. He knew that they were, and applied to a friend for solution of the matter. "Whom have you bribed?" "The contractor was forced to admit that he had bribed no one." "Then go and do it at once," said the other, "begin with the lackey at the door, and don't stop short of the Secretary."

Armed with this advice, the contractor proceeded to the proper office and began by tipping a half crown to the man at the door. This brought him not to the Secretary, but to some subordinate's stenographer. Once in the presence of the stenographer, the contractor unostentiously laid a five pound note on the desk, and propounded his query. The stenographer, with alacrity, referred him to some one else, and that person was also tipped, or bribed, as you prefer to regard the operation. Before the Secretary was reached, eleven persons were seen, and the price was higher with each successive official. Finally, when the contractor came to the Secretary, who is a cabinet officer, the latter touched a bell and presently in came a man that had upon his person eco of the contractor's money. This man brought the papers in the case. The Secretary conferred with him; there was some nodding and frowning, and presently the Secretary turned to the contractor and said: "Make your mind easy; injustice has been done to you; another man's material was inspected by mistake for yours."

The contractor probably did not bribe the Secretary, but the operation cost him a good round sum. It was cheap at the price, however, for half his fortune was staked on the venture.

The gentleman in question was at Chester, looking about the Cathedral and wondering how he should get into the Chapter House. Presently he saw a robed gentleman of respectable aspect approaching, and determined to appeal to him. He in robes explained that the Chapter House was not ordinarily opened to the public, but if his questioner would wait for twenty minutes, until the sitting of the Chapter should end, a peep at the place might be obtained. He was subsequently as good as his word, for he not only showed the American about the Chapter House, but explained intelligently many features of interest. As the pair came out, the American eyed his guide and decided that a half crown was the proper tip. So, thrusting a hand into his pocket, he drew out the coin. But before he could offer it, the guide gently and said in haste: "You't better not put it into the charity box." They parted with apologies on one side and soothing assurances on the other, but the American was not placed entirely at ease when, on pointing out his recent guide to an underling of the Cathedral, he learned that the venerable untipped was the Dean himself. Many years ago, while slavery still flourished in Delaware and many negroes that were not slaves were bound for term of years, a famous old politician became surety for a negro bound boy, accused of some criminal offense. While the master was absent a moment, however, the lad, thinking upon the pains of imprisonment and knowing that he was near the lines of several other States, took to his heels. It meant to the master a forfeiture of bail amounting to several hundred dollars. But he took the simple course of going to the Attorney General, as the prosecuting Officer is called in Delaware, pressing a ten dollar bill into his hand and begging to hear more of the case. He had his way.

A species of tipping that cannot be called bribery is common enough in public offices in this country. A New Yorker visiting a public building in Philadelphia was introduced by the Major to the Captain, who should do the honors of the place. In the course of the inspection the Captain exhibited a pamphlet, which the New Yorker saw that he was expected to buy. He paid his quarter, and continued the tour. When the New Yorker attempted to escape, he was detained while the Captain explained impressively that the inspection had been a much more thorough one than was accorded to the mob of visitors. Surely this could not mean another tip, thought the New Yorker, but as the Captain continued in the same strain, his guest began to think that it could mean nothing else. just organized an Alliance with a
good working membership. There
are six others nearby. This section
of North Carolina has never been
popularly known throughout our State
and its possibilities are not appreciated
by our citizens here.

We are situate amid the finest tobacco belt in the country, many of our
farmers raising tobacco that will net
them $500 on one acre of ground.

wealthy or becoming richer and one
of the great reasons is because some
one else feeds, clothes, and thinks for
our farmers who are not their friends.
We were much instructed and united
into a band of brotherhood by S. A.
Houser last week, and a star of hope
now looms up in the distance for our
emancipation and guidance. We
have great hope in the Farmers Alliance, and the devotion and wisdom
of its membership is the financial salvation of our people in North
Carolina. We need instruction, we
need education, and from you, sir,
much good has been done and much
is yet to be done on this line. The
Alliance men, especially in our immediate section, need to educate our
boys and girls to make farmers and
farmers' wives, and to do this requires
more than simply compelling boy to
stay in the corn field or a girl in the
kitchen. It is necessary for them to
know more science, more arithmetic,

SUNDAY, July 24.-The House to-day passed the bankruptcy bill. Various amendments suggested by the committee &c. were adopted, also a new one providing for enforcing the law of the bankruptcy substitute which is known as a "voluntary bankruptcy bill." The vote was then taken on the Torrey bankruptcy bill, which was then passed, with unimportant amendments, yeas 177, nays 81.

MONDAY, July 25.--Mr. Cannon (Ill.), chairman of the committee on appropriations, presented the sundry civil appropriation bill with Senate amendments, with recommendations relative thereto. The House went into committee of the whole for the consideration of the bill. The point of dispute was the irrigation feature of the Senate amendments. Mr. Payson (Ill.) asked that general debate on all portions of the bill except the irrigation amendment be closed in thirty minutes, and on those amendments two and one-half hours debate shall be allowed. He had. Pending further debate the committee arose, and the House took a vote, making the evening session to be for the deliberation of private pension bills.

FRIDAY, July 26.-The House, to-day, promptly went into committee of the whole for the consideration of the sundry civil appropriation bill. After the Speaker had appointed Messrs. Hill (Fla.), Thompson Co., and Oates (Ind.) as concurrent on the original package bill—the committee having risen for that purpose—the Senate amendments to the sundry civil bill were read serially and concurrence was recommended on several Senate amendments, including the one appropriating $4,000 to be expended at the Chicago breakwater station, and the committee rose with the amendments still pending and the House adjourned.

SUNDAY, July 28.-The House went into committee of the whole for further deliberation of the Senate amendments to the sundry civil appropriation bill. The recommendations of the committee were agreed to with much friction, the bone of contention being the Senate irrigation amendment, which was passed over until the other matters were disposed of. Without disposing of all the amendments, the committee rose and the House adjourned.

TUESDAY, July 29.-The session was held up in debate on the Senate amendments to the sundry civil appropriation bill.
